summaryTr: Osmanlı sadrazamı, zalim Şah İsmail'in sarayına gönderecek korkusuz bir elçi arar ve kimseye boyun eğmeyen Muhsin Çelebi'yi bulur. Çelebi, bütün servetini ortaya koyup meşhur Pembe İncili Kaftan'la Tebriz yoluna çıkar; Ömer Seyfettin'in bu hikâyesi onur, cesaret ve gösterişsiz fedakârlığı anlatır.
paragraphs: ## The Silent Divan

The great hall of the Divan was cool and quiet that spring morning. The Divan was the council of the Ottoman state, where the sultan's ministers met to decide the business of the empire. Coloured light came in through the windows and collected in the deep green of the tiles. The viziers, the ministers of the sultan, sat tired and silent on their high silk cushions and looked at the patterns of the carpet. The old grand vizier, the head of all the ministers, held his long white beard in his thin hand. His dull eyes stared at nothing, as if he were thinking of very distant and very dark things.

"We need a brave man, pashas," he said at last. A pasha was a high officer of the state, a general or a governor. "The Shah of Persia sent us an envoy, a man who carries a ruler's message to another ruler. He came loaded with gold and jewels, but we did not let him kiss our sultan's hand. We allowed him to kiss only the sultan's knee. Without doubt, the Shah will want to pay us back in the same way."
"Without doubt," said one pasha. "Certainly," said another. "Of course," said a third.

The grand vizier saw that everyone agreed, so he spoke more clearly. "Then the man we send must be very brave. He must not be afraid of death. He must stand firm against anything that harms the honour of our state, and he must not bow his head to insults because he is afraid to die."
"Yes!" "Quite right." "Very true."

The grand vizier sat up straight and looked at the nervous ministers, one by one. "Then find me a brave man," he said. "I cannot think of one, not among the clerks, not among the palace officers, not here in the Divan. You think about it too." Nobody said a word. The Divan, a quiet and careful mind inside the huge empire of a pious, peaceful sultan, began to think.
The envoy would go to Shah Ismail, the ruler of Persia. Years later, at the battle of Çaldıran, the Ottomans would defeat this proud and cruel king. But nobody could know that yet.

The sultan, Bayezid, was a gentle man. As a young prince he had spent his days with books, not with horses and swords. He loved poetry and wisdom, and he hated war. His viziers believed that their first duty was never to disturb his peace. Yet on the borders the fighting never stopped, and campaigns followed one another. Worst of all was the east, where Shah Ismail had built a wild empire. Wherever he passed, no tree was left standing, and people said that he drank wine from the skull of a defeated enemy king. Everybody knew that one day he would cross the sultan's border.

In fact, he had already begun. The year before, he had marched into a small border land that was a friend of the sultan. He took its castles, and he killed the ruler's son and grandsons in a way too terrible to describe. The peace-loving sultan did nothing, except to send an army to Ankara.

The Shah was as cunning as he was cruel. He said he was sorry and sent one envoy after another. But Prince Selim, the governor of Trabzon, was not patient like his father. He crossed into the Shah's country, robbed the land and even took the Shah's brother prisoner. Now the Shah's envoy complained about this too. So the Divan could not find the right man. Whoever stood in front of the Shah would certainly be insulted, and if he answered back, the Shah might kill him in some terrible way.

The pasha on the grand vizier's right had not moved all this time. He had sat as still as a gravestone under his tall red-feathered turban. Now the turban moved. "I know a man who is just right for this mission," he said. "His father was my comrade. But he does not accept any government post."
"Who is he?"
"Muhsin Çelebi." Çelebi was a title for an educated gentleman.
The grand vizier did not know the name. "Does he live in the city?"

"Yes, in Üsküdar, across the water. He is fairly rich, and he spends his time reading. He never mixes with great men, and he does not look for rank or favour. Perhaps he thinks that all greatness passes away."
"Strange..."
"But he is very brave. He is not afraid of death. He has fought in many wars for the faith, and there are sword scars on his face."
"Would he serve us as an envoy?"
"I do not know. Would he come to your feet if you called, sir? He owes nothing to the world. To him a shah and a beggar are the same."
"Does he not love his state?"
"I think he does."
"Then we will call him, not for ourselves, but to serve his state."

That evening the grand vizier sent his steward to Muhsin Çelebi's house in Üsküdar with a letter. It said that he wished to speak to him about a matter of state, and that he must come the next morning without fail.
## A Man Who Would Not Bow
After the morning prayer, the grand vizier sat in a small, dim room with heavy curtains, reading papers, when a servant told him that Muhsin Çelebi had arrived. "Bring him here," he said.

Two minutes later the walnut door opened, and a big, cheerful man with a thick curved moustache walked in. His large eyes shone under thin black eyebrows, and the weapon belt at his waist was empty. The grand vizier was used to the bowing of his servants, and for a moment he waited for the man to fall at the hem of his robe. The man did not. The grand vizier had never seen anyone with his chest forward and his head up like this. Even the ministers of the Divan stood bent double in front of him.
"You sent for me, sir," said Muhsin Çelebi in a perfectly natural voice. "What do you want to say?"
"Well... Come, my son, sit down here."

Muhsin Çelebi sat down on the cushion that was shown to him, quite simply, without fear or shame. The grand vizier looked at the papers in his hands and thought, "What kind of man is this? Is he mad?"

But he was not mad at all. Muhsin Çelebi was rich enough not to need anybody. He ran a big farm and a dairy behind the Çamlıca woods, lived honestly, and bowed to nobody. He looked after the poor and the strangers, and there were always guests at his table. He was a believer, but not a fanatic. His only ideal was this: to bow to no one except God, and never to be one servant's servant. The great scholar Ibn Kemal used to say of him, "He teaches me." He was a poet, but he had never written a poem in praise of the powerful. He was past forty, and he had never taken any of the roads to success that opened in front of him. He knew that at the end of those golden roads there was always the same thing: a dirty hem to kneel before.

In his eyes, a human being was something very high and noble, a deputy of God on earth. A dog that wags its tail and licks its master's shoes could be forgiven. But a man? He hated those who climbed to power bent double, swallowing every humiliation. To avoid seeing such people, he had almost stopped going out. Only in times of war did he leave his house, to lead a company of the sultan's horsemen.
"We want to send an envoy to Tabriz," said the grand vizier. "Will you go for us, my son?"
"Yes. We cannot find the kind of man we are looking for."
"Until now I have never taken a post in the state."
"Why not?"

Muhsin Çelebi was silent for a moment. Then he smiled. "Because I do not bow, sir," he said. "I do not kiss hems. The powerful men of our time all rose by bowing and kissing hands and even feet, with a thousand kinds of flattery. So they gather around themselves only people who do the same. Their favourites are low hypocrites and shameless clowns. And when they see a brave, honest, free man, they hate him at once and work to destroy him. Why was Gedik Ahmed Pasha stabbed with a dagger, my pasha?"

The grand vizier did not answer. He pressed his teeth together and crushed the paper in his hand. Even when he was only a governor, nobody of his own rank had spoken to him so plainly. "Is he mad?" he thought again. "What rudeness! I should have his head cut off." He opened his mouth to call the doorkeepers. Then, from some place inside himself that he could not find, he heard a deep voice. It was his conscience. "So you too cannot bear a free and honest word, like all those who rose by flattery! You too want around you not a real man but a dog that licks your feet!"

He closed his mouth. He put the crushed paper down and looked at Muhsin Çelebi once more. He saw the high forehead with the shining mark of a sword across the middle, the strong neck, the large, slightly crooked nose. The man looked like one of the old heroes in the Book of Kings, the great poem of the Persian heroes. Yes, this was a living hero whom no sword had been able to knock down. The grand vizier was a fair man, and he did not drown the voice of his conscience in his pride. "This is exactly the man we are looking for," he said to himself. A man so fearless would never accept an insult to his state out of fear of death.
"We shall send you to Tabriz as our envoy," he said.
"You have so many secretaries and scholars at your side," said Muhsin Çelebi. "Why do you not choose one of them?"
"Do you know who Shah Ismail is?"
"I know."
"Do you love your state?"
"I love it."

The grand vizier leaned back. "Very well, then. This wicked man does not keep the old rule that an envoy must not be harmed. What he cannot do to us on the battlefield, he wants to do to the man we send. He may even kill him with torture. And any insult to our envoy is an insult to our state. We need a man who will not fear for his head, a man who will give that insult back to the Shah, exactly as it was given. If you love your state, you will accept this sacrifice."
Muhsin Çelebi did not think at all. "I accept, sir," he said. "But on one condition."
"What condition?"

"Since this is a sacrifice, it cannot be done for pay. A sacrifice made for the state in exchange for money is only personal profit, whatever it is called. I want no salary and no rank. I will do this service freely."
## The Pink Pearl Kaftan

"But, my son, how can this be?" said the grand vizier. "The Shah's envoy was dressed very richly. Our envoy's horses, servants and clothes must be even more splendid. For all this we will give you several thousand gold pieces from the treasury."

"No," said Muhsin Çelebi. "I will not take one coin from the treasury. I will prepare the splendid horses and servants with my own money. And I will do even more. I will put on my back something that Shah Ismail has never seen in his life."
"What will you wear?"
"The Pink Pearl Kaftan, which is at Toroğlu's, the gold-thread merchant." A kaftan was a long silk coat, and great men wore the richest ones on the most important days.

The grand vizier had good reason to be surprised. The kaftan had been finished a month before, and it was covered with the rarest pink pearls. Everyone in Istanbul had heard of it. Whenever viziers went to Toroğlu to buy it as a gift for the sultan, he raised the price. "Where will you find so much money?" he asked.

"I shall pledge my farm, my dairy and my house," said Muhsin Çelebi. "That means the lenders can take them if I do not pay. I shall borrow ten thousand gold pieces from the merchants, spend two thousand on the horses and servants, and buy the kaftan with the remaining eight thousand."
"But after you come back, the kaftan will be no use to you. It is only a toy for show. You will lose your property and become poor."

"No. Six months later Toroğlu will buy it back from me for seven thousand. With that money I will free my farm. If I cannot pay my other debts, then let my dairy, which my father left me, be given up for the state. One cannot only take from the state. Sometimes one must give a little too!"

The grand vizier said nothing. His wonder grew, and his heart became light. Here at last was the right man. The delicate, fearful, calculating gentlemen of the Divan loved their lives and their property too much. If one of them was sent, he would think about his reward more than the honour of his state, and he would accept every insult. The grand vizier wanted Muhsin Çelebi to stay for a meal, but he could not persuade him. He walked with him all the way to the hall.

In the following months Muhsin Çelebi pledged his farm, his dairy, his house, his shop and his garden. He borrowed money from the merchants. He prepared horses and servants more splendid than anyone had ever seen. He bought the Pink Pearl Kaftan from Toroğlu, on the condition that Toroğlu would take it back for seven thousand when he returned. He left his young wife and his two small children in the house of a relative, with money to live on for six months. Then he put the sultan's letter inside his coat and set out.

Stage by stage, the splendour of the new envoy, and above all the fame of his kaftan, travelled across Anatolia and reached the land of Shah Ismail before him. One day Muhsin Çelebi rode into the fortress of Tabriz in great glory. The people of this small capital loved colour and show, and they stared at the kaftan in wonder.

Shah Ismail had heard of "the Pink Pearl" only in tales. He felt a deep anger toward this rich envoy who owned something he had never seen, and he decided to crush him with insults. Before he received him, he hid his executioners behind the throne. He had the silk cushions and prayer rugs in front of the throne taken away. His viziers stood on his right, and his warriors stood on his left.
## The Court of the Shah

Muhsin Çelebi walked in through the wide open doorway with his head as high and his chest as far forward as always. He took the sultan's letter from his coat, kissed it and touched it to his forehead. Then he held it out to the Shah, who sat on the golden throne like a strange bird of prey, wrapped in piles of red, green and blue silk. Nobody kissed the Shah's foot. His face turned yellow with fury, and he took the letter.

Muhsin Çelebi stepped back and looked around. There was nothing to sit on. He smiled. "So they want to keep me standing here, in a position of respect," he thought. How should he answer this insult? Quickly he took the Pink Pearl Kaftan off his back and spread it on the floor in front of the throne. The Shah, his viziers and his commanders stared at him, stupid with surprise. Then he sat down on the precious kaftan with his legs crossed and shouted in a voice that rang through the pointed dome:

"The great sultan whose letter I have brought is from the family of Oghuz Kara Khan! Since the world was made, none of his ancestors has been anyone's servant. All of them were sultans. All of them were khans. The envoy of a ruler whose family have been rulers since the creation of the world does not stand before any foreign ruler. Because there is no sultan in the world as noble as his own sultan. Because..."

He went on and on, shouting his rough Turkish speech. The Shah understood every word. He went red, then yellow, then purple. The letter shook in his hands. Behind the throne the executioners drew their swords. The courtiers were amazed at their ruler's patience, and some of them began to murmur.

When he had finished, Muhsin Çelebi did not ask for permission. He got up and walked toward the door. The Shah sat frozen, like a stone. The pride that would be broken at Çaldıran had already melted under the burning eyes of this one Turk. "Give him his kaftan," he managed to say.

A warrior ran forward, picked up the kaftan from the floor and caught up with the Turkish envoy. "Here you are," he said. "You are forgetting your kaftan." Muhsin Çelebi stopped and laughed. He turned back toward the hall and spoke in a loud voice, so that the Shah could hear.

"No, I am not forgetting it. I am leaving it to you. In your palace you have no rug and no cushion to seat the envoy of a great sultan. Besides, a Turk never puts on his back again what he has laid on the ground. Did you not know that?"
## The Garden in Kuzguncuk

Muhsin Çelebi galloped back by the roads he had come, day and night. When he rode into Üsküdar, there was not a single coin left in his pocket. He said to his splendid servants, "My children! The horses you ride, the clothes on your backs, the jewelled daggers at your belts, I give them all to you. Do you forgive me for anything I owe you?"
"We do," they answered. "As our mother's pure white milk."

He sent them away and took a deep breath. He did not even go home. He jumped into a boat and went to the grand vizier's house. He said that he had given the letter to the Shah, that he had suffered no insult, and that he had left without waiting for the Shah's permission. The grand vizier had never doubted that he would do his duty well. When the Çelebi stood up to leave, the grand vizier said, "I want to buy it, my son. Is your kaftan here?"
"No, I did not bring it."
"Did you sell it in Persia?"
"No, I did not sell it."
"Was it stolen?"
"No."
"Then what did you do with it?"
"Nothing!"

The grand vizier asked again and again, but he could never understand what had happened to the kaftan. Muhsin Çelebi was not so small-minded that he would be proud of what he had done. The next day Toroğlu came, ready to take the kaftan back for seven thousand gold pieces as they had agreed. Muhsin told him only this: "The kaftan will not come back. Our agreement is finished, and you may take what I owe you from what I own." He did not say where the kaftan was or why. In curious Istanbul, nobody ever learned how, where or why the famous Pink Pearl Kaftan was left behind. The adventure in the palace at Tabriz disappeared into the darkness of history and became a secret.

Without the seven thousand gold pieces, the once rich Muhsin Çelebi could not pay the debts he had made for the kaftan, and he could not free his farm and his dairy from the pledge. The lenders took them. He sold the horse and the jewelled gear that remained from his mission, and with the money he bought a tiny garden at Kuzguncuk. He planted it and harvested it, and he earned bread for his wife and children. Until the day he died, he sold vegetables in the market of Üsküdar. He lived a very poor, bitter life, full of things he did without. But he never bowed his head to anyone. And he never made himself look great by talking about the sacrifice he had made when he threw away his whole fortune at once.

glossary.divan: divan; Osmanlı'da vezirlerin toplandığı devlet meclisi
glossary.envoy: elçi (bir hükümdarın başka hükümdara gönderdiği temsilci)
glossary.kaftan: kaftan; devlet büyüklerinin giydiği uzun, süslü ipek giysi

quiz.q: What did the grand vizier need to find at the beginning of the story?
options: A new sultan for the empire
A rich merchant to lend gold
A brave envoy to send to Shah Ismail
A strong army to defend Ankara
quiz.explainTr: Sadrazam, Şah İsmail'e gidecek ve hakaret karşısında ölümden korkmayacak cesur bir elçi arıyordu.

quiz.q: Why had Muhsin Çelebi never taken a government post?
options: He did not want to bow to powerful men or flatter them
He was too poor to live in Istanbul
Nobody had ever asked him to serve
He was afraid of the Shah
quiz.explainTr: Muhsin Çelebi boyun eğmeyi ve el etek öpmeyi reddettiği için devlet görevine hiç girmemişti.

quiz.q: What was Muhsin Çelebi's condition for going to Tabriz?
options: He wanted a high rank in the Divan
He wanted a large gift from the Shah
He wanted several thousand gold pieces from the treasury
He wanted to do the service without any payment
quiz.explainTr: Muhsin Çelebi, fedakârlığın ücretle yapılmayacağını söyleyerek maaş, mansıp ve ücret almadan hizmet etmeyi şart koştu.

quiz.q: What did Muhsin Çelebi do with the Pink Pearl Kaftan in front of the Shah?
options: He gave it to the Shah as a gift
He spread it on the floor and sat on it
He sold it to the Shah's viziers
He wore it and stood quietly before the throne
quiz.explainTr: Şah'ın sarayında oturacak yer olmadığı için Muhsin Çelebi kaftanını yere serdi ve üzerine oturdu.

quiz.q: What happened to Muhsin Çelebi after he came back to Istanbul?
options: He became grand vizier and lived in a palace
He became the Shah's friend and lived in Tabriz
He lost his money and sold vegetables, and he never boasted about what he had done
He sold the kaftan again and became richer than before
quiz.explainTr: Kaftanı geri alamadığı için borçlarını ödeyemedi; Kuzguncuk'ta küçük bir bahçe alıp ömrünün sonuna kadar sebze sattı ve yaptığını hiç övünerek anlatmadı.
